blocks.title: Abstract
blocks.content:
There can be many competing and contradictory explanations for
a single model prediction, making it difficult to select which one
to use. Current explanation evaluation frameworks measure qual-
ity by comparing against ideal “ground-truth” explanations, or by
verifying model sensitivity to important inputs. We outline the
limitations of these approaches, and propose three desirable princi-
ples to ground the future development of explanation evaluation
strategies for local feature importance explanations. We propose
a ground-truth Agnostic eXplanation Evaluation framework
(AXE) for evaluating

summary.text: Abstract and publication details of "Evaluating Model Explanations without Ground Truth" (FAccT '25, Athens, June 2025). A single prediction can have many contradictory explanations, and current evaluation frameworks either compare against ideal ground-truth explanations or test model sensitivity to inputs. The authors set out the limitations of both, propose three principles for evaluating local feature-importance explanations, and present AXE, a ground-truth Agnostic eXplanation Evaluation framework that needs neither ground truth nor sensitivity analysis. They compare it with baselines and show it can detect explanation fairwashing; code is on GitHub.

summary.text: Introduction, with Figures 1 and 2. Explanations often disagree, and choosing a wrong or deliberately misleading one matters in healthcare, credit and criminal justice. Of about 300 papers proposing explainers, one in seven ran user studies and one in three evaluated only anecdotally. The paper focuses on post-hoc, model-agnostic local feature-importance explanations (such as LIME and SHAP) for tabular models. Figure 1 shows four explainers (Gradients, SHAP, LIME, Integrated Gradients) giving different signed feature importances for one diabetic prediction on the Pima Indians dataset. The authors propose three principles (local contextualisation, model relativism, on-manifold evaluation) and AXE, which judges an explanation good if its important features are most predictive of the model's output, following user research that useful explanations help users predict model behaviour. Disagreement also enables fairwashing, where an explainer hides that protected attributes drove a prediction. Figure 2 contrasts explanation generation with AXE's evaluation.

summary.text: Sections 2.1 and 2.2 and Table 1. Notation: an input x in R^N, a binary classifier m, an explanation e = E(x, m) in R^N of signed importances, a quality metric q in [0, 1] (higher is better), and an aggregate score Q as the average of q over a dataset X. The three principles: local contextualisation (when the datapoint changes, the metric should not always prefer an unchanged explanation), model relativism (likewise when the model changes), and on-manifold evaluation (the score should not change when only off-manifold model predictions change, since many explainers are themselves sensitivity analyses). Ground-truth comparisons violate these: one ground truth per datapoint ignores the model, and one per model ignores the datapoint. Table 1 defines the ground-truth metrics FA, RA, SA, SRA, RC and PRA (which fail the first two principles), the sensitivity metrics PGI and PGU (which fail on-manifold evaluation), and AXE, which the authors mark as satisfying all three.

blocks.title: Prior Approaches
blocks.content:
Explanations can be evaluated using any of the evaluation metrics
defined in table 1. Broadly, these fall into two categories:
(1) ground-truth based metrics compare the generated explana-
tions e with ground-truth annotations e∗, either collected by
humans or inferred using a different proxy [20, 21, 44, 51].
These include Feature Agreement (FA), Sign Agreement (SA),
Rank Agreement (RA), Signed Rank Agreement (SRA), Rank
Correlation (RC) and Pairwise Rank Agreement (PRA) [31].
(2) sensitivity based metrics verify model sensitivity to the in-
puts declared important by an explanation [17, 30,

summary.text: Sections 2.3 and 2.4, prior approaches and the invariance of ground-truth metrics, with Figure 3. Metrics are either ground-truth based (FA, SA, RA, SRA, RC, PRA) or sensitivity based (PGI, PGU); explainers include LIME and SHAP (fitting linear models to synthetic neighbours) and gradient methods (Grad, SmoothGrad, Integrated Gradients, Input × Grad), and the experiments use the OpenXAI benchmark. User studies show useful explanations help predict model behaviour, but few metrics implement this. For linear models the coefficients are often taken as ground truth for every datapoint; with a two-feature model y = β0 + β1X1 + β2X2 and (β1, β2) = (0.7, 0.3), Figure 3 shows large regions of explanations receiving identical scores, violating local contextualisation. Because the metrics are symmetric, the plots are unchanged for any model with β1 > β2 > 0, such as (0.99, 0.01), (0.99, 0.98) or (0.02, 0.01), violating model relativism.

blocks.title: Inherent biases in sensitivity Metrics
blocks.content:
Sensitivity based explainers E like LIME are highly sensitive to
hyperparameters. This facilitates adversarial fairwashing attacks
(section 4.1) [54] and can cause feature importances to switch arbi-
trarily from highly positive to highly negative [40, 49]. Sensitivity
analysis based evaluation metrics 𝑞suffer similar problems.
Metrics like PGI and PGU may simply encode a preference for
particular explainers. We formalize this in the context of synthetic
data. Consider a wide range of explainability measures that measure
some loss, ℓ, defined in terms of the fidelity 𝐹to classifier responses

summary.text: Section 2.5, biases in sensitivity metrics. Sensitivity-based explainers such as LIME are highly sensitive to hyperparameters, enabling fairwashing and sign flips. The authors define a general fidelity loss over synthetic neighbourhoods around each datapoint (Eq. 1) and note that the per-point minimiser of that loss (Eq. 2) is an explainer that scores best by construction: with squared loss and Gaussian neighbourhoods it is LIME, as the variance tends to zero it is the gradient, and with cube-vertex sampling it is SHAP. PGI uses L1 loss with Gaussian neighbourhoods, so it is otherwise interchangeable with LIME and favours explainers built on the same notion of fidelity, violating on-manifold evaluation.

blocks.title: Methodology
blocks.content:
Inspired by previous work (section 2.3) and desiderata from user
studies [4, 7, 9, 12, 25, 45], we consider a simple alternative to
sensitivity-driven methods of XAI evaluation: the important fea-
tures in any explanation should be more predictive of the model
output than the unimportant features. AXE adopts classifier ac-
curacy [28] to measure the predictiveness of the top-n important
features. This “top-n” style formulation, just like prior metrics from
table 1, is considered intuitive for practitioners [2].
For datapoint x and explanation e, the top-n most important
features are the import

summary.text: Opening of Section 3, methodology. The authors' alternative: the important features of an explanation should be more predictive of the model's output than the unimportant ones. AXE measures this as the accuracy of a k-nearest-neighbours model in recovering the model's prediction m(x) from only the top-n features by absolute importance, a top-n formulation that practitioners find intuitive. The choice of k-NN is motivated by feature separability in Section 3.2.

summary.text: Section 3.1, the AXE framework and Algorithm 1. For each datapoint and its explanation, AXE takes the n most important features, trains a k-NN on the dataset restricted to those features with the model's predictions (not the true labels) as target, predicts for that datapoint, and finally reports accuracy against the model's predictions. Using a separate k-NN per datapoint gives local contextualisation, predicting the model's outputs gives model relativism, and using only existing data gives on-manifold evaluation. The k-NN models can be cached (at most N-choose-n distinct ones), other performance measures can replace accuracy, and an area under the curve over all n gives a single score sensitive to the whole importance order. Applied to Figure 1 with k = 5 and n = 4, AXE scores Gradients 0.4, SHAP 1.0, LIME 0.6 and Integrated Gradients 0.8, so SHAP is judged most useful.

blocks.content:

summary.text: Section 3.2, an illustrative example, with Figures 4 and 5. Data are 5,000 points from each of four Gaussians centred at Q = (2, 2), R = (−2, 2), S = (−2, −2) and T = (2, −2), and the model predicts 1 exactly when X1 > 0, so for point Q an explanation favouring X1 (e_a) should beat one favouring X2 (e_b). With n = 1, AXE's neighbours along X2 mix both classes (score about 0.5) while those along X1 are all positive (score 1.0), so AXE ranks e_a above e_b for every k (Figure 5a). PGI perturbing X2 gives a zero prediction gap, and perturbing X1 also gives zero until the perturbation width is large enough to cross the decision boundary, at which point the perturbed points are mostly off manifold and PGI is unstable (Figure 5b). The authors conclude that k-NN avoids off-manifold predictions and ground truth and captures the idea that important features separate classes.

blocks.title: Detecting Explanation Fairwashing
blocks.content:
We simulate a state-of-the-art adversarial attack [54] on explana-
tions in a real-world setting where ground-truths remain unknown.
The attack modifies a model 𝑚, known to be discriminatory, creat-
ing new models 𝑚𝑆or 𝑚𝐿that respectively fool SHAP and LIME
into generating explanations e that show the discriminatory feature
as unimportant. A good explanation evaluation metric 𝑞should
identify manipulated explanations by scoring them poorly.
This attack fairwashes model explanations by hiding discrimi-
natory model behavior. Imagine explanations for the diabetes pre-
diction model figure

summary.text: Section 4.1, detecting fairwashing, with Table 2. The authors replicate the Slack and colleagues attack that modifies a discriminatory model so that SHAP or LIME ranks spurious foil features above the protected one, on German Credit (favouring men) and COMPAS and Communities and Crime (favouring white people). They build explanation sets where the protected feature, a foil, or another feature is most important, and require a good metric to score the protected-feature set higher than each foil set. Over ten model and dataset settings, AXE (n = 1) always passes, with protected-set scores of about 0.96–1.00 against 0.68–0.77 for foils; PGU fails 7 of 10 and PGI 3 of 10, a combined failure rate of 50% against 0% for AXE. The authors read this as experimental confirmation that PGI and PGU share LIME's and SHAP's objectives and violate on-manifold evaluation.

Integrated Gradients (gradient base

summary.text: Section 4.2, comparison with baselines, with Figures 6 and 7. Using OpenXAI, the authors test four datasets (German Credit, COMPAS, Adult Income, HELOC), logistic regression and neural networks, seven explainers (SHAP, LIME, SmoothGrad, Grad, Input × Grad, Integrated Gradients, Random) and all eight prior metrics, using the AUC over n, reporting AXE for k = 1, 3, 5 and 9, inverting PGU, and z-scoring results per metric. Ground-truth metrics are available only for logistic regression, using its coefficients; neural networks get only PGI and PGU. The AXE variants broadly agree with each other, while the ground-truth metrics disagree among themselves. No prior metric clearly separates the Random explainer from the others, and PGI and PGU rank it particularly well, which the authors link to PGI's dependence on perturbation width.

blocks.title: Conclusion
blocks.content:
The ability to measure explanation quality is integral to developing
better explanations, and to engender trust in existing XAI methods.
In section 2.2 we introduced three principles to guide the evalua-
tion of explainers and local feature-importance model explanations:
local contextualization, model relativism, and on-manifold
evaluation, reflecting that explanations should be dependent on
input datapoints, dependent on models, and independent of off-
manifold behavior respectively. We constructed simple examples in
sections 2.4 and 2.5 showcasing the violations of these principles
by prior

summary.text: Conclusion. The authors restate the three principles (explanations should depend on the datapoint and the model and not on off-manifold behaviour), the synthetic examples showing prior metrics violating them, AXE as an operationalisation of the user-research finding that useful explanations help predict model behaviour, the k-NN illustration, the fairwashing experiment (which they believe makes AXE the first metric to detect it perfectly), and the baseline comparison. They argue that lacking a way to choose between explanations undermines trust in XAI and hinders its adoption, and hope the principles and AXE give local explanations a firmer foundation.
